annotations.keyFindings: Among 1,208 patients who chose their setting, completion was 74 percent home-based against 52 percent centre-based; six-minute walk distance rose by 48 metres in completers of both.
annotations.limitations: Patients chose their programme; completion defined differently for the two programmes; non-starters counted differently.

annotations.keyFindings: Remote rehabilitation non-inferior for six-minute walk change at 12 weeks (mean difference minus 6 metres, margin 25); completion 80 percent remote against 71 percent centre.
annotations.limitations: Younger than the usual population; people without a smartphone excluded.

annotations.keyFindings: In 23 trials with 2,890 participants, outcomes were similar between settings and completion slightly higher at home (risk ratio 1.04, 95 percent confidence interval 0.97 to 1.12).
annotations.limitations: Mostly men under 65; completion definitions varied.

annotations.keyFindings: In 652 remote patients, 31 percent dropped out before week six; higher among women (odds ratio 1.42), age 75 or over (odds ratio 1.67) and the most deprived (odds ratio 1.58).
annotations.limitations: One programme; reasons for stopping not recorded.

annotations.keyFindings: Each additional 10 km lowered the odds of completing centre-based rehabilitation (odds ratio 0.91); completion 38 percent beyond 40 km against 63 percent within 10 km.
annotations.limitations: Car access and employment not recorded.

annotations.keyFindings: Applied to the same records of 2,214 patients, six definitions gave completion rates from 41 to 79 percent; attendance-equivalent measures made home and centre programmes most comparable.
annotations.limitations: Four programmes; no outcome beyond completion.

annotations.keyFindings: The 28 women who did not complete cited caring responsibilities, transport and feeling out of place; some preferred home-based rehabilitation, others valued the centre's social contact.
annotations.limitations: One urban hospital; mostly women over 60.

claims.text: In a randomised trial, completion was 80 percent with remote and 71 percent with centre-based rehabilitation.
claims.passage: Completion was 80 percent in the remote group and 71 percent in the centre group.

synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Randomised evidence suggests that remote or home-based rehabilitation gives similar outcomes and similar or higher completion than centre-based programmes in younger, mostly male populations. Observational comparisons where patients choose their setting report larger differences, but completion rates depend heavily on the definition used (41 to 79 percent on the same records), travel distance lowers centre-based completion, and remote dropout is higher among women, older and more deprived patients.
gradeRationale: Randomised evidence is indirect for this population; the observational comparisons are confounded by choice and by inconsistent definitions of completion.
summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; four source-derived claims; overall certainty low.
